name: Old bamboo
lede: Old bamboo is a muted grey-green, the plain English translation of *Oitake-iro*, a traditional Japanese color named for the dulled stalks of mature bamboo.

sections.title: A bamboo stalk's later color
sections.body:
*Oitake-iro* (老竹色) reads literally as "old bamboo color": *oi* for old or aged, *take* for bamboo, *iro* for color [1]. Where young bamboo runs bright green, older canes dull toward grey and olive as they weather, and the traditional name captures that later, quieter stage rather than the plant's first green [1]. Our data carries no further record of which dictionary or era first listed the name beyond the Wikipedia catalogue of Japanese traditional colors [1].

The nearest look-alikes on file are [[ivy-green]] and [[yew-green]], both almost the same shade, and [[ebony|Ebony]] and [[deep-slate-olive|Deep Slate Olive]], both greener [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A close match to this green appears in 1,215 of our 23,781 archived paintings, about 5.1 per cent, with the within-painting lens finding it in 731; that makes it more common than 86 per cent of our named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, at 1.7 times the archive's overall rate (89 paintings), and most often sits as a hidden color rather than a shadow or highlight [3]. Edvard Weie is its most devoted painter here, carrying it in 10 of his 33 archived works, well above the baseline for the museums holding them [3]. The earliest dated match is 1190, as photographed, a floor from the archive's thin early centuries, not a sighting of bamboo in paint that old [3].
